item.title: Social media companies are using AI and face scans to spot more kids on their platforms
item.description:
Of the child safety measures agreed to in Meta’s landmark legal settlement, no category contains more detailed requirements than its commitments on age assurance—and for good reason. No matter how well the protections work, they are of little use if Meta can’t tell which users are kids.

Determining which accounts belong to children is also the linchpin of child safety measures that other companies, including Google, TikTok, and Roblox, are ramping up as public and regulatory sentiment turns against them in the U.S. and other countries.

The Meta settlement—with protections the company says could become industry standards—will give the social media giant a year to refine its approach. But the options are limited, and improving age verification technology presents steep challenges, including navigating privacy implications not just for children but for adults who could have to prove they are over 18.

The $18 billion settlement resolves claims from state attorneys general that it hurt children’s mental health by deliberately designing its Instagram and Facebook platforms in ways that hooked young people’s attention. The agreement announced last week with the Menlo Park, California, company involves 48 states plus the District of Columbia and U.S. territories.

Tech companies lean on AI for estimating ages

In the offline world, people use government-issued IDs to prove they are over 18 or 21, whether they want to get into a club or buy cigarettes. While this technically works online too, many people are not comfortable giving a Big Tech company like Meta or Google access to their driver’s license or passport.

Meta accepts IDs to check ages, and promises to delete them within 30 days. Beyond IDs, though, a growing number of tech companies are using artificial intelligence to try to determine users’ ages. This is not true age verification. While AI can estimate a person’s age, often accurately, it can’t verify a person’s birth date.

Last year, Google began using an age-assurance system for YouTube that relies on AI to differentiate between adults and minors based on their watch histories. Meta does the same.

AI age checks use clues to determine how old someone is. On Instagram, this includes “contextual clues” such as posts about birthday celebrations or school, and things like which posts people like, comment on, or linger on, who their friends are, as well as the times of day they log in. For instance, someone who is offline during school hours would likely be school-aged.

In a blog post last year, Meta said its AI also looks at photos people post for visual cues, including “height or bone structure, to estimate someone’s general age; it does not identify the specific person in the image.”

“By combining these visual insights with our analysis of text and interactions, we can significantly increase the number of underage accounts we identify and remove,” the company added.

Under the settlement, Meta agreed to strengthen its age-checking technology using its own tools, as well as third-party ones, with regular outside audits on how well it is working. The agreement also includes specific goals around false positive rates—that is, minors who are identified as over 18. And if a user is identified as under 13 and kicked off one of its platforms, Meta will check the ages of their friends, too.

Face scans count as age assurance on some sites

Identity verification companies like Yoti and Persona, which work with tech companies like Meta and Roblox, use video selfies people upload to estimate their ages.

The gaming site Roblox, which, unlike social media platforms, allows kids under 13 to sign up, requires players to take a video selfie to estimate their age. Roblox says the videos are deleted after the age check is processed. Users are not required to submit a face scan to use the platform, only if they want to chat with other users.

Some users have reported inaccuracies, and some experts have expressed caution about the reliability of facial age estimation tools, especially for women or certain racial or ethnic groups. But Matt Kaufman, chief safety officer at Roblox, said last year that for people between about 5 and 25, the system can accurately estimate their age within one or two years.

Some websites and social media companies such as Meta have argued that age verification should be done by app store owners, such as Apple and Google, and not individual platforms. This would mean that app stores would have to verify their users’ ages before they allow them to download apps. Unsurprisingly, Apple and Google disagree.

“Billed as ‘simple’ by its backers, including Meta, this proposal fails to cover desktop computers or other devices that are commonly shared within families. It also could be ineffective against pre-installed apps,” Google said in a blog post last year.

Privacy concerns remain an obstacle

Age checks are meant to keep kids out of online spaces that are not safe or appropriate for them, whether that’s social media or adult websites. But critics of online age verification see a worrisome trend toward a less secure, less private and less free internet, where people can be denied access not just to pornography but news, health information and the ability to speak openly and anonymously.

What’s considered harmful to minors can be subjective, and this is where experts believe laws requiring age verification can run afoul of the First Amendment. The question could lead to people being required to verify their ages to access anything, from Netflix to a neighborhood blog.

The digital rights group Electronic Frontier Foundation has been warning for years about “age-gating the internet.”

“(No) matter the method, every system demands users hand over sensitive and immutable personal information that links their offline identity to their online activity,” EFF writes in a blog post. “Once that valuable data is collected, it can easily be leaked, hacked, or misused.”

—Barbara Ortutay, AP technology writer

item.title: Tech giants are trying to obliterate privacy. Australia has a rare chance to take back part of their power | Lizzie O'Shea
item.description:
‘Pervert glasses’ are selling out, tick-a-box consent is broken and the spectre of surveillance is invading all aspects of our lives

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A mere five years after the government first started talking about it, new changes have finally been proposed for the Privacy Act. They could not be more overdue and urgent. “Pervert glasses” are selling out at Kmart, facial recognition technology is proliferating in our everyday environments, and microtargeting for advertising has filled our algorithms with nonsense and toxic junk.

Privacy reform is hugely popular: 93% of Australians say protecting personal information is important to them, and 87% say they are more concerned about their privacy than they were five years ago. But it is practically impossible for us to take personal responsibility for our data footprint, especially in the age of AI. Tick-a-box consent is a broken model. Australians rate protecting our personal information as their number one priority for AI regulation.

Boreal forest stretches for miles and miles across high northern latitudes, covering huge swathes of Canada, Russia, Alaska and Scandinavia. It makes up nearly a third of global forest area and is mainly made up of evergreen trees such as spruce and fir. But this landscape could change.

item.title: Why the Japanese don’t need fat jabs
item.description:
‘You can never be too rich or too thin’: so said Wallis Simpson. Or perhaps Dorothy Parker. Or perhaps Joan Rivers. No one really knows. But whoever said it, Japan appears to have had it engraved on its national escutcheon. Japan is officially the world’s thinnest rich country, with an obesity rate of just 4.3 per cent of the population. By comparison, it’s 28 per cent in the UK and 40 per cent in the USA. A close comparison to Japan is Bangladesh, where the rate is 4.5 per cent - but where one in ten people is dangerously undernourished. These are extraordinary statistics. What on earth is going on?
The most reached-for reason is diet. Japanese food, so it is thought, is healthy and lean.

Lisa, a freelance graphic designer based in Spain, noticed a shift in her work after the release of ChatGPT in 2022. She went from receiving slow one-off jobs creating logos and packaging to an onslaught of requests asking her to fix versions that were generated by artificial intelligence – from sharpening fuzzy images for printing to turning flawed designs into usable files.

By 2025, Lisa, who asked not to be fully named to avoid solicitations, said 90% of her incoming logo and packaging design requests required cleaning up AI-generated content, work that accounted for 60% to 70% of her annual income. But the grind was exhausting. Last week, I finally managed to snatch one read out of the jaws of a hectic summer. On a series of very long-haul flights (highly recommended as a way to break reading droughts), I fell into the world of Simukai Chigudu’s Chasing Freedom: Coming of Age at the End of Empire. I finished the book just as I was landing in Nairobi, Kenya. In a daze, I stepped on to the tarmac in the chill of equatorial winter.

The book was about growing up in post-colonial Zimbabwe and navigating life between the ex-colonised and the ex-colonial power. Imagine matching with someone on a dating app who seems to have it all: charm, wealth, a glamorous lifestyle, and serious intentions about building a future with you.

That was the promise prosecutors say 35-year-old Daejon Love offered to women he met online. Federal authorities recently charged Love and an alleged accomplice with defrauding more than two dozen women of approximately $1.3 million through fictitious investment opportunities.

According to the complaint, Love allegedly posed as a San Francisco 49ers player or wealthy real estate investor, used romantic relationships to gain women’s trust, and then persuaded them to send money. The case is a stark reminder that dating scams often begin not with an obvious request for money but with the careful construction of emotional connection and trust.

The internet has revolutionized dating, and since the COVID-19 pandemic there has been a surge in U.S. adults using apps to find ideal matches. While these apps offer convenience for connecting with romantic partners, they also open the door to online romance scams. Criminals create both deceptive profiles and urgent scenarios to carry out the scam.

The Federal Trade Commission reports that nearly 70,000 Americans fell victim to online romance scams in 2022, with reported losses topping $1.3 billion.

Romance scams exploit people through calculated online social engineering and deliberately deceptive communication tactics. In a series of research projects, my colleagues from Georgia State University, University of Alabama, University of South Florida and I focused on understanding how scammers operate, the cues that may prompt changes in their tactics, and what measures people can take to prevent themselves from being victimized.

How online romance scams work

Online romance scams are not coincidental. They’re carefully planned schemes that follow distinct stages. Research has identified five stages:

  • Baiting victims with attractive profiles.
  • Grooming victims with intimacy.
  • Creating crises to extract money.
  • On occasion, manipulating victims with blackmail.
  • Revealing the scam.

In short, scammers do not swindle victims by chance. They plan their actions in advance, patiently following their playbooks to ensure profitable outcomes. Scammers worm their way into a victim’s heart to gain access to their money through false pretenses.

Federal prosecutors have accused Daejon Love of defrauding women he met via dating apps.

In a previous study, my colleague Volkan Topalli and I analyzed victim testimonials from the website stop-scammers.com. Our research revealed scammers’ use of various social engineering techniques and crisis stories to prompt urgent requests. Scammers leveraged social norms, guilt, and supposed emergencies to manipulate victims. Scammers also paid close attention to communication patterns and adapted their tactics based on victims’ responses. This interplay significantly influenced the overall operation of the scam.

Around the globe, online romance scammers use different techniques that vary across cultures to successfully defraud victims. In my recent research, for example, I looked closely into an online romance scam in China called sha zhu pan, which loosely translates to “pig butchering scam.” These scammers bait and groom victims for financial exploitation through well-structured group setups. Multiple scammers across four groups—hosts, resources, IT, and money laundering—persuade victims through romantic tactics to invest in fake apps or use fake gambling websites, convincing them to pay more and more without ever receiving their money back. Hosts interact with victims, resources people identify targets and collect information about them, IT creates the fake apps and websites, and the money launderers process the ill-gotten gains.

Deterrence and rewards

Like street robbers, online romance scammers can be encouraged or discouraged by a range of situational cues that serve as incentives or deterrents.

Our investigation showed that deterrent messages can significantly affect scammers’ behavior. Here’s an example of a deterrent message: “I know you are scamming innocent people. My friend was recently arrested for the same offense and is facing five years in prison. You should stop before you face the same fate.” Based on live conversations with active scammers online, our recent analysis suggests that receiving deterrent messages reduced scammers’ response rate and their use of certain words, and increased the likelihood that when they sought further communications, they admitted they had done something wrong.

Our observations indicate that scammers not only diversify their approaches to prompt more responses, such as appealing to their romantic relationships, asking for identifying information, and requesting victims switch to private chat platforms, but also use several techniques for getting victims to overcome their misgivings about sending the scammers more money. For example, scammers subtly persuade victims to see themselves as holding more power in the interaction than they do.

Blocking scammers

There are ways for users to defend against online romance scams.

In experimental findings, my colleagues and I suggest online apps, especially dating apps, implement warning messages. An example would be applying linguistics algorithms to identify keywords like “money,” “MoneyGram” and “bank” in conversations to alert potential victims of the scam and deter scammers from engaging further.

In addition, apps can use tools to detect counterfeit profile pictures and other types of image fraud. By concentrating on identifying scammers’ use of counterfeit profile pictures, this advanced algorithm holds the potential to preemptively hinder scammers from establishing fake profiles and initiating conversations. https://www.youtube.com/embed/-HF5UL69eG0?wmode=transparent&start=0 The FBI gives advice on how to protect yourself from romance scams.

How to protect yourself

Online dating app users can take precautions when talking to strangers. There are five rules users should follow to steer clear of scammers:

  1. Avoid sharing financial information with or sending money to strangers.
  2. Refrain from sending private photos to strangers.
  3. Pay attention to spelling and grammar because scammers often claim to reside in English-speaking countries when they actually operate in non-Western countries.
  4. Use image and name reverse searches.
  5. Confide in family and friends if you grow suspicious.

One last piece of advice to empower those who have fallen victim to online romance scams: Don’t blame yourself.

Take the courageous step of breaking free from the scam and seek support. Reach out to your loved ones, trustworthy third-party organizations and law enforcement agencies for help. This support network is essential in helping you restart your life and move forward.

This is an updated version of an article originally published on Aug. 4, 2023.

Fangzhou Wang is an assistant professor of criminology and criminal justice at the University of Texas at Arlington.

item.title: Steve Jobs said great leaders make 1 difficult choice most managers avoid
item.description:
There is a dangerous idea floating around the workplace: If you care about employees, you should avoid making them uncomfortable.

That sounds compassionate. Sometimes it is. Other times, it is managerial cowardice disguised as servant leadership.

Leaders who avoid difficult conversations leave people guessing. And capable employees miss opportunities to improve because nobody respected them enough to tell them the truth.

Steve Jobs addressed this tension in a 2008 Fortune interview. Describing his responsibility as Apple’s CEO, he said:

My job is not to be easy on people. My job is to make them better.

That line lands differently today. Employees are exhausted. Teams are navigating constant change, artificial intelligence is rewriting jobs, and many managers are leading people they rarely see in person.

Yet the essential leadership decision remains the same: Will you prioritize comfort over hard conversations, or will you help push people to grow and become better?

Challenge people and clear the path

Jobs’s full explanation deserves more attention than the famous quote. He described his job as bringing different parts of Apple together, clearing obstacles, securing resources for critical projects, and pushing talented people to improve.

That changes the equation considerably. A leader cannot demand exceptional work while withholding the information, authority, time, or tools required to produce it.

Before questioning an employee’s performance, a leader should ask:

  • Have I made the expected result clear?
  • Have I explained why it matters?
  • Does this person have the authority and resources to deliver?
  • Did I provide useful feedback before the problem became serious?
  • What obstacle have I failed to remove?

Give feedback people can actually use

Telling someone to “step it up” doesn’t make them better. When having crucial conversations with employees, useful feedback is required, but it must be timely and specific. It describes the behavior, explains its effect, and establishes what better performance looks like. The conversation should leave the employee with a path forward rather than a bruised identity.

This matters even more when work is changing quickly. Employees cannot develop new judgment, adapt to unfamiliar technology, or take intelligent risks if every mistake becomes evidence that they do not belong.

The real test of leadership

Making people better is not something leaders do to employees. It is something they pursue with them.

That requires leaders to see potential, name the gap honestly, provide support, and remain accountable for the environment they create. It also means recognizing when someone cannot or will not meet the standard. Human-centered leadership does not require carrying persistent underperformance forever. It requires handling it clearly and fairly.

Jobs’s quote still holds up, provided leaders understand the responsibility hidden inside it. Your job is not to keep everyone comfortable. Your job is to create the conditions in which capable people can do meaningful work, hear the truth, and become more than they were when they arrived.

My advice? Think of one person on your team who is capable of more. Have the conversation you have been postponing, but enter it with this question: “What support or obstacle removal do you need from me to reach the standard we both know you can meet?”

—Marcel Schwantes

item.title: 5 things Freud got right about your brain
item.description:
Below, Mark Solms shares five key insights from his new book, The Only Cure: Freud and the Neuroscience of Mental Healing.

Mark is a neuroscientist who took the unusual step of also training as a psychoanalyst. For 40 years, he has used the tools of modern neuroscience to test and refine psychoanalytic theory. A pioneering figure in neuropsychoanalysis, he conducted research that uncovered key brain mechanisms involved in dreaming, reshaping our understanding of the sleeping mind. He is the science director of the American Psychoanalytic Association.

What’s the Big Idea?

Freud should not be dismissed as an outdated or discredited thinker. Many of his core insights anticipated modern neuroscience, and the task now is to update and correct psychoanalysis using contemporary scientific evidence.

Listen to the audio version of this Book Bite—read by Mark himself—in the Next Big Idea App, or buy the book.

1. Freud was a neuroscientist

Freud spent 23 years doing neuroscientific and neurological research. During that time, he published more than 200 titles, four of which were books. He contributed to the discovery of neurons, the basic element of the nervous system, in the 1880s. In the 1890s, when the synapse was discovered—that’s the junction that connects neurons—Freud was the first person to interpret it as the site where memories are formed.

In 1895, Freud formulated the idea that neurons that fire together wire together. This is now known as Hebb’s law [Donald Hebb was a Canadian psychologist], even though Hebb formulated this law decades later. Freud discovered the origin of one of the cranial nerves, then called the acoustic nerve, in the brain stem. We now call it the vestibular-cochlear nerve. Every medical student learns the anatomy of these cranial nerves.

Freud was one of Europe’s leading experts on a movement disorder known as cerebral palsy. In 1891, he published a breakthrough book on the brain mechanisms of language, showing that language is the product of a functional system distributed across many different brain regions. This provided the transition to psychoanalysis because language function is a psychological function.

2. Many of Freud’s controversial discoveries are now conventional wisdom

Functionalism was a scientific novelty when Freud introduced it: the idea that we are studying functional systems, which are virtual things. The introduction of functionalism into cognitive neuroscience—the mainstream view nowadays—is generally attributed to [the American philosopher Hilary] Putnam in the 1950s. Again, decades after Freud introduced the concept.

Freud also introduced the idea of multiple memory systems in 1896. The idea is that our memory system is not unitary, but rather divided over multiple different systems, each of which functions in a different way. The idea is attributed to other researchers, again, decades after Freud introduced it. Freud said there must be at least three memory systems, which he defined as conscious, preconscious, and unconscious. That’s exactly how we divide the multiple memory systems today. The mainstream cognitive neuroscience model divides them into short-term memory (conscious), declarative long-term memory (preconscious), and nondeclarative long-term memory (unconscious).

Speaking of the unconscious, that was another novelty of Freud’s: the idea that mental functions can be unconscious. When Freud introduced this idea, it was considered an oxymoron. In those days, mind and consciousness were synonymous. The idea that large portions of our mental life occur unconsciously is now mainstream.

What is called predictive processing today—a highly influential framework developed by [the British neuroscientist] Karl Friston—was, again, actually anticipated decades earlier. Predictive processing is basically the same as wishful processing. It is the idea that once you’ve had an experience of satisfaction, you try to repeat it based on how that satisfaction was achieved in the past. Conversely, when you have a noxious experience, you try to avoid it by not repeating the circumstances that produced it. This is a fundamentally Freudian idea, and Friston acknowledges this debt.

The same is true of embodied cognition, which was often presented as a contemporary development. Freud was the first to emphasize that cognition is embodied—that human beings are a species of animal, and the mind works on behalf of the organism as a whole, learning how to meet its needs in the world.

“We often forget that this was once a novel Freudian idea.”

Freud also pioneered the idea of critical periods in mental development. Consider infantile amnesia. We cannot remember the first two years of our lives because the cortical memory systems that Freud called the preconscious, and we now call declarative long-term memory, have not yet fully matured.

Similarly, the idea that traumatic experiences in early childhood can lay the foundations for later psychopathology was a Freudian idea. Today, it is widely recognized that adverse childhood experiences can increase vulnerability to conditions like depression. Yet we often forget that this was once a novel Freudian idea.

Freud also approached studying the brain from a subjective point of view, asking, in effect, what it’s like to be this brain. Today, the need to account for subjective experience is associated with what [the Australian philosopher and cognitive scientist] David Chalmers famously called the “hard problem of consciousness,” a problem generally regarded as being at the cutting edge of contemporary neuroscience.

3. The talking cure is a highly effective medical treatment

In medicine and psychiatry, we measure treatment effectiveness in terms of what’s called effect size. An effect size of 0.2 is considered mildly effective, 0.4 moderately effective, and 0.8 highly effective. On average, psychiatric medications have an effect size around 0.4.

Talk therapy has an effect size of between 0.7 and 0.8, placing it in the highly effective range. The same is true of short-term psychoanalytic psychotherapy. Randomized controlled studies have established an effect size of about 0.8, but that figure does not take account of something known as the “sleeper effect.”

With most psychotherapies, symptoms are substantially relieved by the end of treatment, but at follow-up—months or years later—they tend gradually to return. Psychoanalytic psychotherapy appears to follow a different pattern. Not only do the improvements persist after treatment ends, but they may also continue to increase.

“Talk therapy has an effect size of between 0.7 and 0.8, placing it in the highly effective range.”

Long-term psychoanalytic psychotherapy has been reported to produce even larger effect sizes, 0.9 and above, with follow-up effects exceeding 1.0—which is off the charts. The effectiveness of psychoanalytic therapy is comparable to that of established medical interventions, such as glucose-lowering medications for diabetes or the HPV vaccine in preventing cervical cancer.

4. Psychiatric medications suppress symptoms while talk therapy treats the root cause

One of the greatest fallacies to have gripped the public imagination is that psychiatric symptoms are caused by chemical imbalances in the brain. In the book, I review the evidence against this theory, including research recently summarized in Molecular Psychiatry by the eminent psychiatrist Joanna Moncrieff. The evidence suggests that the chemical-imbalance theory, at least in its familiar form, is simply not supported.

Psychiatric medications are important; they can relieve symptoms. But symptom relief is not the same as curing an underlying condition. When treatment is discontinued, symptoms may return, and these medications can also carry significant side effects and withdrawal effects. Many were not originally intended to be taken for years or even decades, yet long-term use has become increasingly common.

Freud offered a fundamentally different account. On his view, emotional symptoms arise when emotional needs are not adequately met. Psychoanalytical treatment, and talk therapies in general, aim to help patients find better ways of recognizing and meeting those needs. If unmet emotional needs are causing the symptoms, then addressing those needs means addressing the causes rather than merely alleviating the symptoms.

5. Freud got some things wrong

The main thing Freud got wrong was his theory of sexuality. He made the point that the motive for sexual behavior is not reproductive success. He argued that pleasure-seeking is what motivates sexual behavior. He pointed to masturbation as supporting evidence for this claim, because it is a clearly sexual act that cannot result in babies. Another example he used is homosexual intercourse, which also cannot result in reproductive outcomes. Freud was convinced that people perform sexual acts ultimately because they enjoy them.

Then Freud went further: If the purpose is purely the pursuit of pleasure, then sexuality is not a reproductive function but a pleasure-seeking function. From there, he concluded that anything done purely for the sake of pleasure is sexual behavior—which is a total redefinition of the word “sexual.” This is what led Freud to say, “Look at a baby at the breast. Initially, it suckles to meet nutritional needs, but once it’s satiated, it carries on sucking. Why? For pleasure. Therefore, it’s sexual.” That’s the origin of his idea of oral sexuality, which he says is a component of the overarching sexual function.

“Scientists make mistakes, especially pioneers like Freud, but we don’t cancel them.”

Nowadays, we would say that a baby continues to suckle at the breast after its nutritional needs have been met because continued suckling meets the need for attachment. Attachment bonding is not a form of sexuality. It’s pleasurable for the child to have its caregiver present, but that’s because it meets a need all its own. It turns out there are many psychological needs like this.

There are many different pleasures in the brain and many different chemistries that mediate those pleasures. Sexual chemistry is only one type. It makes no sense to call all forms of pleasure components of one overarching function.

Scientists make mistakes, especially pioneers like Freud, but we don’t cancel them. We don’t cancel Newton because he didn’t know about quantum physics. We don’t cancel Darwin because he didn’t get everything right. Instead of canceling Freud, we should continue the job he started. It’s not just a matter of proving Freud right or wrong, but rather of finishing the job.

item.title: I attempted to institute a ‘no-shame’ rule in my work, and it was a lot harder than I expected
item.description:
When I’m having an unproductive day, I hear the most annoying and unhelpful voices rattling around in my head. It’s usually a variation of taunts about how I should have gotten up earlier or shortened my morning routine. Then it turns into how I better be “on it” for the rest of the day, and tonight I must get an early night’s sleep, because I’m way behind and the only way to get everything done is to be diligent about sticking to my calendar at all costs.

I hear how stupid it sounds, and I know it’s not helpful. But for as long as I can remember, a bad day at work always triggers a variation of shame-filled voices. And while I know what I need to do to combat it, I resent how much energy that takes. I’d rather use that energy to get my work done!

Last month, I worked on an article where I interviewed women who pursued “cozy entrepreneurship.” For one of the women, that meant following a set of rules and boundaries that optimized her business around her life, rather than the other way around. The first rule was to eliminate shame. That meant not letting harsh voices dictate what she should and shouldn’t do.

It seemed an overly simplistic way to tackle a problem that had been bugging me for most of my working life, but I was determined to try it.

First week—varying degrees of success

The first week I tried it, I experienced varying degrees of success. When I got what I needed in terms of sleep, movement, nutrition, and social interaction, I didn’t find it too difficult. Naturally and unsurprisingly, I was also usually more productive when all of these elements of my life were present, so it wasn’t like there was a lot to shame me for.

It became a lot harder when life’s inconveniences showed up. Maybe it was a bad night’s sleep, an illness, an appointment that took longer than I expected, or a public transport delay that ended up putting me an hour behind schedule. While my logical brain knows that this is exactly when I should be practicing self-compassion, that’s when I’d hear voices in my head telling me to stop making excuses.

The problem with eliminating shame (or any emotions)

One of the things that has always baffled me is that shame isn’t as much of a factor in other areas of my life, like my health and relationships. It hasn’t always been that way, but I’ve worked hard to get to a point where self-compassion takes over shame.

And I’ve seen the positive impact that it’s had on both. My relationships are richer and deeper, and I’ve maintained a consistent routine around sleep, nutrition, and exercise for many years now. But unlike work, I don’t beat myself up when life happens and I fall short of those standards, because I know it’s temporary.

I asked Lydia Woodyatt, a psychology professor at Flinders University in Adelaide, Australia, about why I seem to have a problem with eliminating shame when it comes to work. The first thing she told me is that my goal shouldn’t be to eliminate it.

“I don’t think that’s a healthy way to think about emotions,” she says, “because our emotions are a natural thing that our body does.” Instead of trying to make shame go away, she suggests treating our feelings like a signal. “With shame, what we can do is challenge our natural emotions towards shame.

“Shame is fundamentally our body giving us an alert that we’re at risk of social devaluation or exclusion,” she says, so we often feel shame “in context where we’re violating shared group norms or a sense of what it means to be a good group member.” High achievers or high-productivity people at work, she adds, “are often part of social groups that care about those things, and that might come from their childhood, their parents, their friends, the groups that they’re part of at work. And that drives the set of social norms and standards that [they] internalize.”

Why shame persists in some areas of life but not others

With my specific situation, Woodyatt noted that working in a freelance and highly autonomous environment means I am the sole driver and producer, and this can create added pressure. The nature of my work also makes it feel more high-stakes, since I’m constantly exposing it to public and social evaluation.

Then there’s the identity part. When your identity is so highly centralized around a specific part of your life, it can feel like your whole world is crumbling when that part isn’t going as well as you hoped. She gives the example of elite athletes who struggle in retirement or when something derails their performance.  

A healthier way to deal with shame

Rather than eliminating shame, Woodyatt recommends reframing the situation to move away from the “all-or-nothing” approach.

For example, say you’ve had a misunderstanding with someone and they’ve cut contact, and you notice shame creeping in because you realized you’d violated your values of respecting others. Shame would make you feel bad about the situation, but a more helpful approach is actually to ask yourself: How can I repair that? How can I live according to that value now? What can I do to reinforce that value?

“We can’t always immediately fix the exact thing that caused the shame,” Woodyatt says, but “we can try and address the value threat that’s kind of undermining that experience.”

What I’m trying instead

What all of this tells me is that instead of getting rid of shame, I need to have a conversation with it.

The thing is, shame has absolutely no response when I tell it: No, I’m in danger of social exclusion if I don’t meet my own arbitrary standards of productivity. I also try to think about what my high-achieving and productive friends would say to me. They would probably tell me that one not-as-productive day doesn’t define me, and also that beating myself up about it isn’t doing anything to improve the situation.

“The research is pretty consistent that if you hold perfectionistic standards, that’s actually not helping your performance,” Woodyatt says. “And if you start to let those go, your performance doesn’t actually drop; you’re still actually good at what you’re doing, you still have internal standards towards quality,” she continues.

The difference is, “you don’t have to beat yourself up in order to maintain those standards.”

item.title: How to navigate a values conflict at work as a leader
item.description:
In general, your satisfaction with work is driven in part by whether your organization has a mission that is aligned with your values and goes about its work in a manner that is consistent with how you choose to live your life. I have written about the impact of values conflicts at work broadly before, but there are several specific problems that arise when you are a leader and the organization wants to do things that are a mismatch to your deeply held commitments.

When your organization wants to do something or pursue a project that violates a value you hold dear, it creates a significant impact for leaders. For one thing, you are more strongly identified with the organization by others than people lower down in the food chain. For another, you are likely to feel pressure to conform by other leaders. In addition, leadership roles are well-respected and well-compensated, so there are pressures not to rock the boat.

In addition, as a leader, you may feel like you have enough influence to change the direction the organization is going, so you may continue to do things you find problematic in the hope of blunting the impact of what you see as a bad path. Here are four steps to take if you find yourself in this position.

1. Understand your red lines

The problem is that the longer you do things that conflict with your values and engage with colleagues who have no qualms with that work, the more that psychological mechanisms of conformity begin to influence your thinking. At some point, you come to think of the world more similarly to your colleagues and may be less likely to see what you’re doing as problematic.

So, if you’re going to go down the path of continuing your work as a way of trying to provide resistance, you should write out a list of lines that you do not want to cross. Keep that list handy, because you will find yourself compromising. Rather than being led down a path in which you slowly give up on your values, use your initial list as a reminder of what your past self valued. That may help you to know when it is time to throw in the towel and leave the organization.

2. Maintain a firewall

It can be a noble effort to work behind the scenes to change a course of action you find problematic, but you have to be careful to protect the people who work for you. You should engage with people in parallel roles and those above you in the food chain. Have discussions. Argue your views. You may even ally with others in leadership roles you find to have similar views to your own.

Resist the urge to engage your team members in this effort, though. By virtue of your position, you are going to be persuasive to others who want to please you because you are their boss. If the organization persists in doing things you disagree with, you may ultimately find yourself leaving the organization (of your own volition or otherwise). You will not be able to protect anyone on your team from the repercussions of their actions. It is one thing if people choose to act on their own accord, but another thing entirely to encourage people to act along with you unless they understand the potential consequences of their actions.

3. Listen, empathize, and counsel

If you have a values conflict with the organization, it is likely that others share your reservations. They may even come to you to discuss it. For the reasons I just discussed, you should be careful sharing your own opinion on the situation. Start by listening with empathy and letting those team members know that you hear their concerns. You can advise them on the courses of action they may choose to take and counsel them on the potential consequences of what they choose to do.

If you choose to share your own opinion about the situation, then also share the approach you are taking. There are risks and benefits to speaking up about courses of action you disagree with. It is important that you and others in the organization be willing to stand up for what you believe in. But, everyone should do so with full awareness of the consequences and a willingness to suffer those consequences. For many people, the prospect of losing a job because they disagree with an organization’s course of action seems abstract, but it can have a significant impact on someone’s life when it becomes a reality. People who want to resist should ensure that they are mentally and financially prepared.

4. Respect different decisions

Finally, recognize that values conflicts also create true internal conflicts. People who choose to fight a course of action they disagree with should respect those who make a different decision. Your internal calculus and risk tolerance are different from those of your colleagues. You would certainly want others to respect the decisions you make, and you should accord others the same respect.

item.title: How AI could kill ‘corporate ick’
item.description:
Imagine a workplace where you spend less time attached to a keyboard, worrying about how to word an email, write a report, craft a LinkedIn post, polish a presentation deck, or sound professional enough in an office-wide memo. 

Instead, you stop hunching over a keyboard and start talking your way through a written correspondence, the way you might with another person. 

Such a workplace may not be as far off as you imagine, according to Calum MacDougall, president of the enterprise division at audio equipment brand Jabra. Whether office culture actually keeps pace, though, is another question.

“The keyboard was invented in 1868, when Ulysses S. Grant was president—and it’s probably the only thing invented in 1868 that you still have in your office right now,” MacDougall tells Fast Company. “So it seems natural at some point that technology should be able to overtake it to create something new.”

AI will become more and more important in the workplace, he says, which is far from a controversial opinion. But he believes “the future will be here quicker than we think.”

“The way that you will want to communicate with your [AI] agents will be increasingly in the way that you communicate with your human colleagues,” he says. “Which is by voice.”

Less corporate speak, more creativity

MacDougall argues that AI could make work more conversational, and that, in turn, could promote creativity. 

For starters, it’s easier to talk than it is to type. The average person types 40 words per minute but speaks much faster. (Depending on the source, estimates range between 100 and 160 words per minute.) So, people can naturally share more context, much more rapidly, when communicating verbally.

There’s also the question of how we formulate our thoughts. MacDougall argues that when people type, especially in a professional context, they tend to naturally self-edit. He predicts that rather than carefully crafting emails, prompts, and documents, conversational AI will encourage future workers to brainstorm, ask questions, and collaborate with it much as they would a colleague.

There is some research to support the idea that speaking and writing lend themselves to different kinds of thinking. 

A literature review published on the open-access research platform SSRN at the end of last year by AI educator, speaker, and author Bryan Cassady—in collaboration with researchers at Cornell University—argues that speaking ideas aloud can increase both the volume and divergence of thought, particularly during the early stages of development.

Research from IBM in 2024 also explored how highly conversational AI interfaces could support creativity in the workplace, finding that “creativity emerges in the hybrid interstitial conversational space between human and AI.”

But what happens to decades of workplace norms built around polished written communication? 

Younger workers are already questioning some of the conventions of the modern workplace. The “corporate ick” has become shorthand for Gen Z’s distaste for performative professionalism—from useless jargon to office attire and the pressure to put on a buttoned-up workplace façade.

“It’s just much more practical and efficient to talk to people like normal people, which we quite often don’t do in business,” MacDougall says. “To create a more casual, almost egalitarian way of working, which is more open—I think the technology can enable that.”

Pamela Pavliscak, an adjunct assistant professor at the Pratt Institute’s School of Information who studies human-computer interaction, tells Fast Company that with conversational AI, people can start with unfiltered spoken thoughts or use their own notes to talk through ideas.

“The really interesting thing that I’m seeing with voice interactions is that it can stay a little messy for a while, and sometimes the really interesting ideas come from that messiness,” she says. “It makes it easier to separate the idea of brainstorming and generating ideas from the idea of presenting them formally.”

Since so much corporate communication is rigid and templated, “this can feel liberating,” Pavliscak says.

The downside of thinking out loud

There is a paradox here, though, Pavliscak explains. Conversational AI might free workers from thinking in corporate-speak, only for AI to translate those messy thoughts back into something boring.

“While it might free people up from thinking in corporate, the end result will likely be smoothed out by AI into something more blandly professional,” Pavliscak says.

Voice-based AI, however, may preserve some of the personality that corporate communication has encouraged workers to water down. “Voice keeps that imperfection, that human signal that is so important,” Pavliscak says. Many leaders say humanity is going to be vital in an AI-led future, potentially giving value to those imperfections.

Getting there may take some adjustment. Keyboards have been around for a long time, and speaking to AI introduces its own privacy concerns. There are also questions about the separation between the individual and the company when workers are encouraged to verbalize thoughts to corporate AI systems. “Do they then own my thoughts?” Pavliscak asks. “It feels very intimate.”

Generally, if people are seen talking out loud to themselves in the workplace, it can be a little awkward. One potential solution is technology that can detect extremely quiet speech, such as the voice-to-text accessibility app Wispr Flow, which says it can “keep up with fast talkers” and handle speech as quiet as a whisper. But as MacDougall says: “You can develop the technology fast, but then there has to be the cultural element to be ready to adopt it.”

Overall, a multimodal workplace could give workers more flexibility and autonomy over how they work. The keyboard is unlikely to disappear overnight—or maybe ever for some people. More likely is a multimodal future where workers move between speaking, typing, and other ways of interacting with AI, depending on what they’re trying to get done.

In this world, the messiness we’ve traditionally been encouraged to edit out of our working lives may turn out to be an asset rather than a bug.
